title: Green Ferns Beside the Path
description: Notice the green leaves, damp ground, and cool shade around woodland ferns.
cardDescription: Notice the green leaves, damp ground, and cool shade around woodland ferns.
focus: These clues stay with things visible on a woodland walk: leaves, roots, soil, and nearby rocks.
solvingTip: Begin with a color, weather word, or short plant part.
words: Green woodland plant with divided leaves and no flowers
Green plant part spreading out from the fern
Place protected from direct sunshine by the trees
Slightly wet, as the ground around these ferns is
Small soft green growth on a woodland rock
Water falling from clouds onto the woodland plants
Color of the fern's fresh leaves
Narrow way followed by a woodland walker
Plant part taking up water from the ground
Hard natural object beside the woodland fern
Not very warm, as a shaded woodland spot may feel
Covered with water after a shower
Stalk supporting part of the fern's growth

answerNotes.FERN: Ferns do not produce flowers; their leaves can have many small divisions.
answerNotes.LEAF: A leaf is part of the plant rather than the soil beneath it.
answerNotes.SHADE: Shade describes the light conditions, not a plant species.
answerNotes.DAMP: Damp is less strong than soaked or flooded.
answerNotes.MOSS: Moss is a different kind of plant from the larger fern beside it.

title: Acorns Under an Oak Tree
description: Look beneath an oak for acorns, their little caps, fallen leaves, and familiar tree parts.
cardDescription: Look beneath an oak for acorns, their little caps, fallen leaves, and familiar tree parts.
focus: The acorn is the oak's nut. Its small cap sits at one end, above the smooth nut itself.
solvingTip: Try a short tree-part word before the nut's name.
words: Oak nut often found on the ground in fall
Tree whose fallen nuts wear little caps
Small rough covering at one end of an acorn
Hard-shelled fruit such as an acorn
Flat tree part that may fall beside the acorns
Large woody arm extending from the oak's trunk
Small thin woody shoot on the tree
Protective outside covering of the oak's trunk
Tree part growing beneath the ground
Season when many ripe acorns drop
Part inside an acorn that can begin a new plant
Common color of a ripe acorn
Fall from a branch onto the ground
Area sheltered from the sun beneath the oak

answerNotes.ACORN: An acorn contains the seed from which a new oak may grow.
answerNotes.OAK: Oak identifies the tree, while acorn names its fruit.
answerNotes.CAP: Cap is the everyday word used here for the acorn's cup-like covering.
answerNotes.NUT: An acorn is a type of nut rather than a berry.
answerNotes.LEAF: Oak leaves have different shapes depending on the kind of oak.

title: A Pine Cone on the Path
description: Study a conifer through its needles, cone scales, and the woody growth around them.
cardDescription: Study a conifer through its needles, cone scales, and the woody growth around them.
subtheme: A Pine Cone on the Path
focus: Pine cones carry reproductive structures rather than forming flowers like a rose. Seed-bearing cones and pollen-producing cones have different roles.
solvingTip: Use the clue’s part or process: leaf, seed covering, sticky material, or airborne powder.
words: Tree group that includes pines, spruces, and firs
Slender pointed leaf of a pine
Sticky substance produced by many conifers
One overlapping segment of a woody pine seed cone
Powdery reproductive material released by male pine cones
Conifer whose familiar leaves are long narrow needles
Reproductive structure associated with a pine tree
Plant beginning carried beneath a pine cone's scales
Protective covering on a pine trunk
Small branch segment bearing needles or cones
Moving air carrying much pine pollen
Hard material forming the trunk beneath its covering
Pointed end of a pine needle
Compact growing point at the end of a shoot

answerNotes.CONIFER: Conifers include familiar cone-bearing trees; the group is broader than pines alone.
answerNotes.NEEDLE: A pine needle is a leaf, not a thorn or a detached cone scale.
answerNotes.RESIN: Resin differs from watery sap in composition and behavior, though the words are sometimes loosely confused.
answerNotes.SCALE: Seed-cone scales protect and carry the seeds; a scale is not the whole cone.
answerNotes.POLLEN: Pollen-producing cones have a different role from the larger seed-bearing cones familiar on the ground.

title: Mushrooms After a Woodland Shower
description: Spot mushrooms through their caps, stems, shapes, and the damp places where they grow.
cardDescription: Spot mushrooms through their caps, stems, shapes, and the damp places where they grow.
focus: The clues focus on what a walker can see. Mushrooms are fungi, while nearby moss and trees are plants.
solvingTip: Look for the short words describing shape and weather.
words: Growth often shaped like a cap on a stem
Upper part of many mushrooms, above the stem
Stalk supporting the top of many mushrooms
Slightly wet, as the woodland ground is after rain
Place out of direct sunlight beneath the trees
Water falling before the woodland walk
Tree material on which some mushrooms grow
Loose earth beneath the fallen leaves
Narrow walking route through the woods
Soft green plant growth near a woodland mushroom
Fallen tree part lying on the forest floor
Not large, as a tiny mushroom may be
Circular in outline, as some mushroom caps are
Earthy color seen on many woodland mushroom caps

answerNotes.MUSHROOM: A mushroom is part of a fungus rather than a flowering plant.
answerNotes.CAP: Cap describes the top rather than the stalk supporting it.
answerNotes.STEM: Not every mushroom has the same shape or a clear separate stem.
answerNotes.DAMP: Damp conditions describe the scene rather than identify a mushroom species.
answerNotes.SHADE: Shade is a condition in the surroundings, not a part of the mushroom.

title: Wildflowers Along a Woodland Path
description: Meet woodland flowers through clear names and recognizable plant features.
cardDescription: Meet woodland flowers through clear names and recognizable plant features.
focus: These clues focus on selected plants rather than treating every flower as a garden annual. Common names can describe shape, color, or the time a flower is noticed.
solvingTip: Look for a completed common name or a count of a distinctive flower part.
words: Woodland flower commonly recognized by three petals and three leaflike bracts
Low-growing flower group including purple and white woodland kinds
Common flower name suggesting a blue hanging bell
One colored segment of a flower's corolla
Frond-bearing plant growing beside woodland flowers
Open flower noticed along the woodland path
Green flat plant part beneath a flower
Absorbing organ anchoring a woodland plant
Reduced direct light under woodland trees

Plant support holding a flower above the ground
Season when many woodland wildflowers bloom before trees fully leaf out

answerNotes.TRILLIUM: The characteristic groups of three help explain trillium's name; the structures below the flower are botanically bracts.
answerNotes.VIOLET: Violet can name a plant or a color; the flower group includes more colors than the name suggests.
answerNotes.BLUEBELL: Bluebell is used for different plants in different regions; the clue concerns the familiar common-name shape.
answerNotes.ANEMONE: Wood anemone is a familiar common-name combination; anemone alone names a larger plant group.
answerNotes.PETAL: Petals belong to the flower itself, while leaves or bracts around it have different roles.
